analysis.one_liner: Provides free adult vaccines to uninsured adults and bans Medicaid copays for vaccines.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in any committee or on the House floor; it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal program giving free recommended vaccines to adults without insurance, purchased by the government and delivered through states, clinics, and correctional facilities. It would have banned Medicaid copays for recommended adult vaccines, required federal employee health plans to cover adult immunizations without a deductible, and barred employer plans from cutting the vaccine coverage they had in 2008. It also funded $500 million in state immunization grants and ordered studies on vaccination rates and shortage planning.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured adults, who would be entitled to federally recommended vaccines at no charge for the vaccine itself; Medicaid enrollees, who could no longer be charged copays for recommended adult vaccines; federal employees, whose plans would have to cover adult immunizations and waive deductibles; and people in prisons and jails and patients at community health centers, who would be covered under the program.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an entitlement for 'vaccine-eligible adults' — the uninsured, patients at federally qualified health centers and public clinics, and people in correctional institutions — to receive federally recommended vaccines without charge for the vaccine, with states receiving the vaccines free of charge.
Prohibits Medicaid providers from imposing copayments or cost-sharing for federally recommended adult vaccines, removing a price barrier for low-income patients.
Requires all Federal Employees Health Benefits Program plans to cover adult immunizations and waive any deductible for those services.

Bars employer group health plans from reducing adult vaccine coverage below what they provided as of mid-2008, and authorizes $500 million in grants to states for free immunization programs, public education, and shortage planning.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a mandatory (direct-spending) federal program to purchase and deliver vaccines and pay providers an administration fee, plus the cost of the education campaign and state grants. Employer health plans and insurers would bear the cost of maintaining existing vaccine coverage levels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The vaccine purchase program is written as direct mandatory spending — an open-ended federal obligation that takes effect before annual appropriations — which is the kind of automatic spending that drew budget objections to similar health entitlements.

The free-vaccine program only applies to adults who are uninsured with respect to the vaccine and reaches them mainly through federally qualified health centers, public clinics, and correctional institutions, so insured adults with high cost-sharing and adults without a nearby participating provider would not benefit directly.
States must apply to participate and, if they had vaccine-coverage insurance mandates, must certify they have not weakened them — an administrative condition that could leave some states out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is straightforward: adult vaccination rates in the United States were and remain low, and cost is a real barrier for people without insurance. The cost is real federal spending, but vaccines are among the cheaper preventive measures per case of disease avoided. The bill's main design weakness is that it helps the uninsured through a separate public channel rather than expanding coverage, leaving insured adults with unaffordable cost-sharing largely on their own.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2007 and sent to four House committees, which sent it to their health subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on December 13, 2007.

The House referred it to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Oversight and Government Reform — and the committees referred it to their health subcommittees in December 2007 and February 2008.
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Uninsured adults gained nothing because the program never started, and the parties that would have borne its costs — the federal budget, employer health plans, and Medicaid programs charging copays — were spared the new requirements. Vaccine makers lost a new guaranteed government purchaser only in the sense that the program never launched; the status quo prevailed across the board.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no program was created

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Oversight committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to health subcommittees, and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no partisan split is recorded; the sole sponsor was a Democrat and no member of either party cosponsored.

industries.note: The government would buy qualified adult vaccines in bulk and distribute them free to providers, creating a large guaranteed purchaser for makers of flu, shingles, and other adult vaccines. The bill never passed, so the gain never materialized.

industries.industry: Employer health plans and health insurers
industries.note: Group health plans would be barred from reducing adult vaccine coverage below mid-2008 levels, and federal employee plans would have to cover immunizations and waive deductibles. The cost is modest but the requirement prevents plans from trimming this benefit.

industries.industry: Community health centers and public clinics
industries.note: Registered providers would receive vaccines free of charge plus a Medicare-schedule payment for administering them, adding revenue and supply to safety-net clinics.
